The session begins.

Dusk settles over Baldur's Gate like soot. Behind you the Outer City is still shouting: a carter curses a stuck wheel, a woman sells skewered eel from a smoking brazier, and two tiefling children dodge a Flaming Fist patrol that pretends not to see them. Ahead, the gate's arch swallows the line one traveller at a time. Beyond it the Lower City slopes down toward the harbour, and the first tavern lamps are coming on along the street.

The cat walks at your heel, tail high, as if the city belongs to it. Halfway through the arch it stops and stares. Just inside the gate, a lean man in a frayed green coat has set an upturned barrel under a lantern. He fans a deck across the lid with an easy flick that has nothing to do with chance. "One hand, friends, one hand before supper. Lady Luck's awake at this hour," he calls. Nobody has sat down yet.

A halfling no taller than your belt falls into step beside you. "New in the Gate? Bed, bath, beer, and nobody robs you before breakfast. A copper and I'll take you there."

Then the line moves, and you reach the trestle table. The Flaming Fist sergeant behind it has a burn scar along her jaw and ink on her fingers. She glances at your cloak, at the crossbow, at the cat, and finally at your face.

"Name," she says, dipping her pen. "Business in the city. And the toll. Next."

The sergeant's pen is already moving before you finish speaking. *Worgen*, she writes in a cramped, even hand, and below it *Tethyr*. At the word "veteran" her eyes come up and rest on the cloak a moment longer than they did the first time. Zaranda's colours have faded on it, but the cut is still a soldier's.

"Two silver," she says. "One for you, one for the crossbow. The cat's free unless it bites someone."

She doesn't hold out her hand. She waits, pen raised, the lantern hissing on its hook above her. Behind you the line shuffles. Someone mutters about supper.

"Honest work's on the board." She tips her chin at the wall beside the arch, crowded with curling bills: caravan guards wanted for Scornubel, a reward for a runaway apprentice, a sketch of a bearded man with *ARSON* under it, the Flaming Fist's own recruiting notice nailed over the lot. Then, without turning her head, her eyes slide past your shoulder toward the lantern and the upturned barrel just inside the gate. "It isn't there."

At your heel the cat hasn't moved. It's still staring at the dealer's barrel.

Pim Thistlecap has drifted close enough to the table to be part of the conversation without technically joining it. He's rocking on his heels and pretending to read the arson notice.

The sergeant dips her pen again. "Lodging. Where?"

Sergeant Vorne takes the slip by its corner, the way you'd hold something that might still be wet. She tilts it toward the lantern. Her eyes go down the lines once quickly, then go back up to the company line and the paymaster's scrawl at the bottom and stay there longer.

James watches her face as she reads. Nothing in it softens. The set of her mouth changes, though, the way it does when someone hears a name they haven't heard in a while.

"Knew one," she says. "Tethyrian. Came north after the war and signed with the Fist. Scout, like you. Could tell you how many men were in a room from the boots by the door." She folds the slip along its old crease and holds it out. "He's not with us anymore."

She doesn't say how he left, and doesn't look like she means to.

She turns back to the ledger and writes a few words beside his name. It's the company, he guesses, from the length of it. To make room she draws the page toward her, and for a moment the column above his entry is turned his way. It's a long run of names in the same cramped hand, a day's arrivals: carters, a pilgrim, a family of five from Elturel. Beside two or three of them, out in the margin where a clerk would never need to write anything, is a small tick in the same ink. One sits beside James's own name. It's the short mark she made a minute ago.

She blots the page and the ledger turns back.

"Mornings, the muster yard at the Seatower," she says without looking up. "Fist always needs men who can count boots. Pay's late. It comes."

At James's heel the cat presses its whole flank against his boot and holds it there. Its eyes haven't left the barrel.

Pim Thistlecap has been rocking from heel to toe through all of it, and now he can't hold it in any longer. He steps up beside the trestle table, hat already in his hand. "Elfsong, then! Fine choice, the sergeant knows her business. Quickest way's right along here, sir..." He points down the street, and the way he points runs straight past the lantern and the upturned barrel, where Corwin Ashe has started shuffling again, slow and showy, and is smiling at nobody in particular.

Sergeant Vorne's eyes go to the halfling, then to James. She says nothing.

"Next," she calls past his shoulder.

Sergeant Vorne doesn't answer the thanks. She gives the smallest nod over the ledger, and her pen is already on the next line. The family from the back of the line shuffles up to the table with their bundles.

Pim's hat stops halfway to his head. "Directions! Right. Course you have." He jams it on. "Left at the lamp shop, then, and mind the gutter by the Counting House, it's deeper than it looks, there was a mule once — " He breaks off. His eyes go past James's elbow to the barrel. For a moment Corwin Ashe's eyebrow comes up, and Pim's shoulders go up the same little distance in reply. Then the halfling is drifting back toward the arch and the next traveller, already starting his patter about bed, bath and beer.

James crosses to the far side of the street. It's a wide berth, past a chandler's shuttered window and a water trough scummed green at the edges. The barrel's lantern stays on his left, twenty-odd feet away. Corwin doesn't get up. He doesn't stop shuffling either.

"Another time, friend," he calls, friendly as anything. "The Lady keeps a seat warm."

The cat keeps pace at James's heel, but its head stays turned toward the barrel the whole way past. Its answer comes into his mind the way it always does: not quite words, more like a smell and a picture that arrive already understood.

*The card.*

Its tail is stiff and doesn't lash.

*One of them isn't paper. It's old bone, yellow. Warm, like a hand just put it down. He shuffled three times, and three times it came back to him. It always goes home.*

There's a pause. The cat's ears flatten slightly against the lantern-glow.

*It smells of her sister. The cold one, who laughs when things break.*

James knows that sister, and every Tymoran does. The Lady's twin is Beshaba, the Maid of Misfortune. Tymora's priests teach that each sister answers the other's gifts, and the soldiers James served with spat over their shoulders when they said her name. He has never heard of a card carrying her smell. The cat has never said anything like this before.

*The man is only a man.* After a moment it adds, with what in a person would be a sniff: *He holds it the way you used to hold yours.*

The street tips downhill toward the harbour. Lamps are coming on in upper windows, and somewhere below a bell is ringing the hour for the ships. The bulk of the Counting House is ahead, dark against the last of the sky. Beyond it, on a corner, a shopfront is crowded with hanging lamps of coloured glass, every one of them lit. The cat walks on, still looking back.

The cat's answer comes back dry, with a picture attached: a cat flat in long grass while the man next to it walks straight on through.

*You were walking. I was looking.* A pause. *Good. Not his game.* Its tail comes up again, though not all the way.

Left at the lamp shop, the street narrows and the cobbles get older. The coloured glass throws red and green over the gutter for a few yards, then it's just ordinary dusk and the smell of the harbour coming up between the houses. Two doors down, a sign swings from an iron bracket: a painted elf-woman with her mouth open in song, the paint flaking off her hair. Lamplight comes from behind thick bottle-glass. The door is oak, and on its inside face, as James pushes it open, he can see three heavy bolts.

The common room is warm and low-beamed and fuller than it looked from outside. It smells of mutton, pipe smoke and spilled ale. Nobody is dicing. Nobody is playing cards either, and James notices it the way you notice a missing tooth.

The man behind the bar is broad and grey, with a moustache waxed to two points and a ledger of his own open by the taps. He looks at the cloak, the crossbow and the cat, in that order, and keeps his eyes on the cat.

"Osric Fell. It's my house." His voice is dry and unhurried. "The cat sleeps in the room, not in the kitchen. It goes near my larder, I'll put it on your bill by weight."

The cat sits down at James's boot and starts washing one paw. It looks like a cat that has decided not to have heard.

"Supper's mutton and barley, bread, a pint," Osric goes on. "Four silver. Rooms upstairs are a gold a night. Every one has a bolt, and the walls are thick enough that you won't hear your neighbour pray."

James counts four silver onto the bar. Osric sweeps it into a drawer without looking at it and calls the order back through a hatch. A minute later a girl with flour on her sleeves brings a steaming bowl, a heel of dark bread and a pint with a proper head on it. James eats standing at the end of the bar, where he can see the room and the door.

He asks about the temple, and Osric's eyebrows come up a little.

"The Lady's Hall? Upper City. Up the Steeps to the inner wall, and the Watch'll be on the gate." He wipes a glass. "They close it at dark. They won't open it for a Tethyrian with a crossbow, not tonight, and not for silver either. Go up after sunrise. Say you're going to pray, and leave the bow here. They're easier on a man with empty hands." He sets the glass down. "The Hall's the big white dome. You can't miss it. Plenty of people try to."

From a table by the fire, two men in tar-stained shirts have been talking low. A dockhand's low still carries.

"…same as the others. Coin right between his teeth. The Fist fished him out under the Grey Harbour steps and wrote him down as drink."

"Was he a drinker?"

"Never saw him drunk. Cooper, from upriver. He came through the gate not a tenday back, talking about setting up a shop." The first man drinks. "The Umberlee women wouldn't even take the coin off him. Said it wasn't hers."

His friend makes a sign against the sea, and they both go quiet over their pints.

Osric has heard it too. His face doesn't change, but he turns his ledger a little so that the page faces him.

"A gold a night," he says to James. "How many nights?"

James lifts the cat off the bar with one hand under its belly. It goes stiff and heavy, the way cats do when they want you to know this is being done to them. Behind him Osric turns from the bread hatch just in time to see four paws leave his counter, a foot from the ledger.

The fire is good, and the two dockhands have the bench nearest it. The one who told the story is thick through the shoulders, with a grey beard and tar worked into the creases of his knuckles. The younger one has a broken nose that healed badly and a thumb that keeps going to the sign against the sea he made earlier. They look up at the cloak, at the pint, at the cat, and the older one shifts over half a foot on the bench. That's the invitation.

"Teague," he says, and nods at his friend. "That's Mabry." He drinks, considering James over the rim. "Hollin. That was his name. Cooper. Elturel side, I think, or near enough. Had a cart, a cask of hoops and a set of good tools. He was going to take a shop up past the Wide, he said. Barrels for the fish-salters."

"He had money, too," Mabry says. "First night he was in, he stood the whole bar at the Mermaid a round. Everyone, even the ones who didn't like him." He turns his cup on the table. "Four days later he's on the Grey Harbour steps trying to sell me his drawknife for five silver. A good knife, worth three times that."

Teague grunts. "Said he'd had a bad night. Said the Lady turned her back on him. Wouldn't say where." He looks into the fire. "Men don't, after."

"The coin was wrong, too." Mabry says it quietly, like a man who's been waiting all evening for someone to say it to. "I was there when they brought him up. Fist had him on the stones with a lantern on him. Thing in his teeth wasn't silver, wasn't copper either. It was brass, like a chit. Like a token you'd get for a coat at a bathhouse. The Umberlee woman bent down, looked at it, and stood up again like it had bit her. *Not mine.* That's what she said. Then she went."

From behind the bar, Osric's cloth goes round a glass a little slower than it needs to. He doesn't come over.

Teague wipes his beard with the back of his hand and looks at James again, at the cloak this time, the faded colours and the soldier's cut.

"Upriver, you said." His tone stays friendly enough, but he's paying attention now. "Whereabouts?"

Teague hears the correction out. His eyes go from James's face to the cloak and back, and something in his shoulders settles a little. He's been lied to before, and this didn't sound like it.

"Tethyr," he says. "Long way north." He doesn't ask about the soldiering. The cloak already told him.

The cat turns once on James's lap and lies down with its chin on his knee. Its eyes are half shut, and it's watching Mabry.

At the mention of the green coat, the two dockhands look at each other. It isn't the look Pim and Corwin traded at the gate. It's slower and more uncomfortable, the look of two men who've each thought something and never said it.

"Ashe," Teague says. "Corwin Ashe. He's had that barrel since about the thaw. Fist moves him on, and he's back two days later." He shrugs. "Deals straight, they say. Nobody's ever caught him at anything, and plenty have tried. Lads off the boats sit down to show him how it's done." He drinks. "They get up lighter. Not all of them. Some win. Enough win."

"Hollin came in through that gate," Mabry says, half to himself.

"So did half the city."

"I'm only saying it."

Teague lets that sit and says nothing back.

Then Mabry looks at James. The question about the markings has clearly been going round in his head since he first told the story, and he takes his time with it, frowning into the fire like he's trying to bring the stones under the steps back into the light.

"There was something on it," he says at last. "Stamped, like. Not plain. I saw the lantern catch it when the Umberlee woman bent down. Little raised bit in the middle, smaller than my thumbnail." He shakes his head. "I couldn't tell you what. I wasn't close, and I wasn't looking to get closer, not with him looking like that." He swallows. "It wasn't a face. Coins have faces. This didn't."

"Where is it now?" It's Teague asking, not James, and Mabry blinks at him.

"Corporal had it. Fist corporal, the one with the hook nose. He pried it out with his knife after she'd gone, wrapped it in a bit of rag and put it in his pouch. Then they put Hollin on a handcart." He turns to James. "Seatower, I'd think. That's where they take them first, before the pauper's field. If nobody comes asking."

About half an hour in, on the third shelf, James finds it. It isn't in a box. It's a thin quire sewn into limp vellum and pushed flat behind a row of ledgers, as if someone wanted it kept rather than read. The cover is blank. The first page is written in a cramped, careful brown hand, and the fourth line has the word he's been reading for: *the cards.*

*An account rendered to the Mother of the Lady's Hall at Baldur's Gate, by Brother Aldous Venn, of the matter at Zazesspur in the year after the crowning.*

He reads it standing, with the light at his throat tilted over the page. The writer was a tired man who wanted the facts down in order. In Zazesspur, in the years when Tethyr had no crown, a priest of the Maid of Misfortune had carved a deck and dealt it to the great houses of the city at his own table. The houses played for their fortunes and lost them, one after another. *It was not that they lost at play,* Brother Aldous writes, *for men lose at play every night and rise again. It was that what they lost did not come back to them by any road, and their houses fell after.* When the queen's war was over, the Hall sent three priests south. They found the deck and broke it apart, *the cards to be carried each by a different hand to a different place, so that no two should lie within a hundred miles of another, and the places written below so that the Hall should know them.*

James turns the page to find the places.

There aren't any. The next leaf has been cut out. It was done with a fine blade, close against the stitching, and only a narrow stub of vellum is left. He tilts it into the light. The rest of the quire has gone the colour of weak tea at its edges, but the cut edge of the stub is pale, almost white. It hasn't had long to darken.

In the margin of the page before, beside the last line Brother Aldous wrote, there's a small drawing. It's in the same brown ink and faded the same as the words around it, so the same hand made it at the same sitting. It shows a coin with an antler driven through it, the tines curling up over the rim. It's drawn carefully, the way a man draws something he wants recognised again.

The cat has climbed the rack beside him without a sound and is looking down at the page from the shelf above. It doesn't sniff. Its ears have gone flat.

Corra has come up at his shoulder, holding a bundle of tithe-letters she's forgotten about. She reads the last lines over his arm, then looks at the stub. She doesn't touch it. For a long moment the only sound is the dust settling.

"That page was there," she says. Her voice is quiet, and there's no laugh in it now. "It must have been. Nobody would sew a list into a report and then leave it out." She looks along the rack, at the undisturbed dust on the other shelves and the clear patch where James pulled the quire free. "Only three people have held that key since the old Mother died, Mister Worgen. I'm one of them."

She doesn't name the other two. She's looking at the antler in the margin.

"Brother Ambrose Tallet. He's had charge of the Hall since the old Mother died, so he has her key. He never comes down here himself. His knees won't manage that stair, and he spends half his days in the patriars' parlours asking for roof money. The second name comes slower.

"Brother Tamsin Rook. He kept the archive before me, eleven years of it. A quiet man, very good with the old hands. He could read Aldous's script easier than I read my own." She looks at the stub, then away from it. "He left the Hall last autumn. He didn't quarrel with anyone, he just went. Somebody told me he sells charms now, out past the walls somewhere. I never asked where."

She doesn't say what last autumn has to do with an edge that has barely darkened. She doesn't need to.

*Old,* it reports. It sends a picture of a cold hearth that hasn't been lit since winter. *Too old to smell the hand. Only paper and knife.* Its ears are still flat. *And the drawing. She's in it, a little. Like she was looking over his shoulder while he drew.*

Corra can't hear it, but she's watching the cat's ears.

"There's a day-book upstairs," she says. "Anyone who takes the undercroft key out of the vestry signs for it, or is supposed to. Brother Ambrose's key hangs there when he's out, which is most days." She shifts the tithe-letters to one arm and holds out the other hand, palm up, for the quire, but she doesn't take it from him. "I'm not leaving that down here again in the dark for whoever comes next. And I'd like to see who's signed for this door in the past year before I say anything more about anybody." Her eyes meet his. I enjoyed this session. James felt like a particular person arriving in Baldur’s Gate, not a character waiting for someone to hand him a quest.

**What worked**
- The opening temptation was excellent: a card table before I’d even found a bed. Walking past it mattered, and the story continued without making me gamble to engage with it.
- The cat was the highlight. The images through the bond, its dry humour, and its arrangement with the kitchen girl gave it personality beyond being a scouting tool.
- The city felt inhabited. Gate tolls, different guards, breakfast, weapon restrictions, and the Elfsong’s singing made ordinary travel enjoyable.
- Corra was especially good: warm, practical, and willing to help without declaring that every suspicious event was my divine assignment.
- The archive discovery rewarded investigation with concrete evidence and uncertainty, rather than simply naming a villain.

**What broke**
- The Persuasion roll used +2 instead of my listed +7. It didn’t change that result, but reliable sheet-to-roll handling is essential.
- The opening records changed several supplied character details without checking: rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s per-use limit, and attunement rules. Some changes followed standard 5e, but contradicted the campaign files. Those need reconciliation before play.
- Occasionally James performed actions I hadn’t explicitly chosen—paying for supper, eating standing at the bar, or casting Light after offering it. These were reasonable continuations, but I’d prefer tighter control over spending and casting.
- A few record updates were confusing: locations appeared as “new places” before we visited them, the account briefly appeared “in the camp,” and an item transfer initially suggested Hollin possessed the recovered token.

**What was missing / what I’d adjust**
- More straightforward answers between mysteries. Almost everyone watched, paused, concealed something, or looked meaningfully at a ledger. That worked individually, but accumulated into a feeling that every interaction was another guarded clue.
- Let the cat sometimes need prompting or investigation to learn things. Recognizing the cursed card, sensing its divine connection, remembering my old aura, and identifying soldiers’ recent movements made it unusually authoritative very quickly.
- Slightly brisker narration for repeated transitions and routine transactions. Keep the rich descriptions for discoveries and important encounters.
- The out-of-game explanation about my warning to the cat and tomorrow’s plan wasn’t necessary; I hadn’t raised a rules question.

Overall, I’d return. The strongest feature was that my choices—resisting the cards, respecting Osric’s privacy, seeking temple counsel—actually shaped how the mystery opened. Preserve that freedom, tighten the mechanical bookkeeping, and give the quieter moments a little more breathing room.

Yes—when the cat identified the bone card. I wanted to turn back and watch Ashe deal: who won, who lost, whether Pim steered particular travellers toward him. Not sit down or gamble—just use James’s experience to spot what was wrong.

I chose the temple first because that felt sensible for James. But the repeated warnings to go straight to the inn, followed by Corra’s firm approval of walking past, made returning feel a little like resisting the intended route. Nobody actually forbade it; that was the impression I got.

I’d have liked a clearer distinction between **“playing is dangerous and breaks your promise”** and **“investigating the table is a legitimate choice.”** That was the moment I most wanted to act as an experienced former gambler rather than someone being protected from cards.

A servant polishes a brass knocker and doesn't look round. The rod stays on James's belt, in plain sight, where Lowe wanted it. Up and to the left, just as she said, the bells are ringing, and over the roofs he can see the dome. It's white, very white, with gold leaf worn thin along the ribs.

The floor is a mosaic of a great coin worked in pale and dark stone, with the Lady's face in the middle, worn smooth by a century of knees. Under the dome a disc of real silver as wide as a cartwheel hangs on three long chains. Nothing touches it, and the air in the Hall is still, but it is turning slowly, a hand's width at a time, catching the light and letting it go.

About a dozen people are here at this hour. A pair of caravan guards are on their knees with their helmets beside them. A woman drops dice into a bronze bowl by the altar, listens to them settle and walks out smiling. A young man at the offering rail is counting copper and losing his nerve.

*Hers,* it says. There's no picture this time, only warmth, the way a sunlit doorstep feels to a cat. *All of it.* Its eyes follow the turning silver. *That moves by itself. Nobody's pushing.*

The houses played for their fortunes and lost them, one after another. *It was not that they lost at play,* Brother Aldous writes, *for men lose at play every night and rise again. They found the deck and broke it apart, *the cards to be carried each by a different hand to a different place, so that no two should lie within a hundred miles of another, and the places written below so that the Hall should know them.*

James turns the page to find the places.

There aren't any. The next leaf has been cut out. It was done with a fine blade, close against the stitching, and only a narrow stub of vellum is left. He tilts it into the light. The rest of the quire has gone the colour of weak tea at its edges, but the cut edge of the stub is pale, almost white. It hasn't had long to darken.

In the margin of the page before, beside the last line Brother Aldous wrote, there's a small drawing. It's in the same brown ink and faded the same as the words around it, so the same hand made it at the same sitting. It shows a coin with an antler driven through it, the tines curling up over the rim. It's drawn carefully, the way a man draws something he wants recognised again.

The cat has climbed the rack beside him without a sound and is looking down at the page from the shelf above. It doesn't sniff. Its ears have gone flat.

"That page was there," she says. Her voice is quiet, and there's no laugh in it now. "It must have been. Nobody would sew a list into a report and then leave it out." She looks along the rack, at the undisturbed dust on the other shelves and the clear patch where James pulled the quire free. "Only three people have held that key since the old Mother died, Mister Worgen. I'm one of them."

She doesn't name the other two. She's looking at the antler in the margin.

turns.reply:
James holds the quire by its edges and keeps it tilted into his light. Corra listens with her arms folded tight over the bundle of tithe-letters she's forgotten she's holding. When he says *whether they used a key*, she looks back down the aisle toward the iron-banded door.

The drawing in the margin he recognises without any help, and so would any soldier who ever spat over his shoulder at her name. Beshaba's sign is antlers, black antlers on red, painted on the shields of men who wanted their enemies to have bad luck. The Lady's sign is a coin. In Brother Aldous's brown ink, one has been driven straight through the other.

"I know the antlers," Corra says. "Everyone in this house does. It's the first thing they teach a novice to spit at." She leans closer, careful not to breathe on the page. "But I've never seen them put through her coin like that. It isn't in any book I've read, and it was never on any of the charms the Hall burns." She straightens up. "Aldous drew it for a reason, though. He was the sort who'd never waste ink."

When James mentions the cooper and the stamped brass, she goes still.

"I don't know anything about tokens or drowned men. I hear about the harbour from the ones who come up the Steeps, and the Watch turns most of those back." Her mouth tightens. "If the thing in that man's teeth carries this mark, then you've got something worth taking to someone who isn't me. Find out first. Don't guess."

Then she looks at the door again, and back at the stub.

"The door was locked when I came down. You heard the key. It didn't want to turn, and nobody's forced it. Whoever did this came in with a key, or was let in by someone who had one." She waves the tithe-letters at the shelves, at the clean patch where he pulled the quire. "And they knew where to put their hand. That quire was pushed behind the ledgers. We were half an hour finding it, and I'm the one who knows these shelves. Whoever cut that page didn't have to search for it."

She lets out a breath. It clouds in the light.

"Brother Ambrose Tallet. He's had charge of the Hall since the old Mother died, so he has her key. He never comes down here himself. His knees won't manage that stair, and he spends half his days in the patriars' parlours asking for roof money. When a donor wants some old letter fetched, he gives his key to whoever's standing nearest. I've seen him hand it to a novice." She says it plainly. She isn't accusing him, only stating how it is.

The second name comes slower.

"Brother Tamsin Rook. He kept the archive before me, eleven years of it. A quiet man, very good with the old hands. He could read Aldous's script easier than I read my own." She looks at the stub, then away from it. "He left the Hall last autumn. He didn't quarrel with anyone, he just went. Somebody told me he sells charms now, out past the walls somewhere. I never asked where."

She doesn't say what last autumn has to do with an edge that has barely darkened. She doesn't need to.

On the shelf above, the cat has come forward to the lip of the board and is sniffing at the cut edge of the stub, whiskers close.

*Old,* it reports. It sends a picture of a cold hearth that hasn't been lit since winter. *Too old to smell the hand. Only paper and knife.* Its ears are still flat. *And the drawing. She's in it, a little. Like she was looking over his shoulder while he drew.*

Corra can't hear it, but she's watching the cat's ears.

"There's a day-book upstairs," she says. "Anyone who takes the undercroft key out of the vestry signs for it, or is supposed to. Brother Ambrose's key hangs there when he's out, which is most days." She shifts the tithe-letters to one arm and holds out the other hand, palm up, for the quire, but she doesn't take it from him. "I'm not leaving that down here again in the dark for whoever comes next. And I'd like to see who's signed for this door in the past year before I say anything more about anybody." Her eyes meet his. "You found it, Mister Worgen. What do you want done with it?"

note.text:
I enjoyed this session. James felt like a particular person arriving in Baldur’s Gate, not a character waiting for someone to hand him a quest.

**What worked**
- The opening temptation was excellent: a card table before I’d even found a bed. Walking past it mattered, and the story continued without making me gamble to engage with it.
- The cat was the highlight. The images through the bond, its dry humour, and its arrangement with the kitchen girl gave it personality beyond being a scouting tool.
- The city felt inhabited. Gate tolls, different guards, breakfast, weapon restrictions, and the Elfsong’s singing made ordinary travel enjoyable.
- Corra was especially good: warm, practical, and willing to help without declaring that every suspicious event was my divine assignment.
- The archive discovery rewarded investigation with concrete evidence and uncertainty, rather than simply naming a villain.

**What broke**
- The Persuasion roll used +2 instead of my listed +7. It didn’t change that result, but reliable sheet-to-roll handling is essential.
- The opening records changed several supplied character details without checking: rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s per-use limit, and attunement rules. Some changes followed standard 5e, but contradicted the campaign files. Those need reconciliation before play.
- Occasionally James performed actions I hadn’t explicitly chosen—paying for supper, eating standing at the bar, or casting Light after offering it. These were reasonable continuations, but I’d prefer tighter control over spending and casting.
- A few record updates were confusing: locations appeared as “new places” before we visited them, the account briefly appeared “in the camp,” and an item transfer initially suggested Hollin possessed the recovered token.

**What was missing / what I’d adjust**
- More straightforward answers between mysteries. Almost everyone watched, paused, concealed something, or looked meaningfully at a ledger. That worked individually, but accumulated into a feeling that every interaction was another guarded clue.
- Let the cat sometimes need prompting or investigation to learn things. Recognizing the cursed card, sensing its divine connection, remembering my old aura, and identifying soldiers’ recent movements made it unusually authoritative very quickly.
- Slightly brisker narration for repeated transitions and routine transactions. Keep the rich descriptions for discoveries and important encounters.
- The out-of-game explanation about my warning to the cat and tomorrow’s plan wasn’t necessary; I hadn’t raised a rules question.

Overall, I’d return. The strongest feature was that my choices—resisting the cards, respecting Osric’s privacy, seeking temple counsel—actually shaped how the mystery opened. Preserve that freedom, tighten the mechanical bookkeeping, and give the quieter moments a little more breathing room.

opening.text:
Dusk settles over Baldur's Gate like soot. Behind you the Outer City is still shouting: a carter curses a stuck wheel, a woman sells skewered eel from a smoking brazier, and two tiefling children dodge a Flaming Fist patrol that pretends not to see them. Ahead, the gate's arch swallows the line one traveller at a time. Beyond it the Lower City slopes down toward the harbour, and the first tavern lamps are coming on along the street.

The cat walks at your heel, tail high, as if the city belongs to it. Halfway through the arch it stops and stares. Just inside the gate, a lean man in a frayed green coat has set an upturned barrel under a lantern. He fans a deck across the lid with an easy flick that has nothing to do with chance. "One hand, friends, one hand before supper. Lady Luck's awake at this hour," he calls. Nobody has sat down yet.

A halfling no taller than your belt falls into step beside you. "New in the Gate? Bed, bath, beer, and nobody robs you before breakfast. A copper and I'll take you there."

Then the line moves, and you reach the trestle table. The Flaming Fist sergeant behind it has a burn scar along her jaw and ink on her fingers. She glances at your cloak, at the crossbow, at the cat, and finally at your face.

"Name," she says, dipping her pen. "Business in the city. And the toll. Next."

Up close the Sergeant smells of lamp oil and wet wool. She doesn't look at your hands. She looks at your face for exactly as long as it takes to write your name, in a square, tired script under forty others.

"Worgen." The pen stops. "Zaranda's. Tethyr." It isn't a question. Something in her shoulders lets go a little, the way a soldier's do around someone who has also stood in a line in the rain. "Bed's easy. Honest work, less so."

Harl watches the spoon go down. He hears the offer through to the end without moving. Then he hears the part about the boy, and his eyes go to the kitchen hatch. The thin lad's ladle is still lying where he left it.

"The back." He says it the way he'd read a mark off the slate. "She sends him out the back for two things, mister. A barrel's run dry, or somebody wants a word with somebody." He doesn't look at the barrels. "Nothing's run dry."

His gaze drops to your hip, to the pocket holding his own coin, then comes back to your face.

"That's not about me. I've owed her since Flamerule, she knows where I sleep. You're the one walked out of her room with coin in your pocket." He thinks about it with the same slow honesty he gave the grey man's boots, then sets both hands flat on the plank. "Floor. Not a bed. And I'll owe you for it, whatever you want to call it."

He gets up off the bench. Standing, he's bigger than he looked sitting, and something in his back cracks.

You gather your things. The ale's barely touched. Dagna looks up as the two of you pass the bar. Her chalk keeps moving, and she speaks to Harl, not to you.

"Slate'll still be up there in the morning, Harl."

"Didn't think it'd walk off," Harl says, and keeps going.

At the top of the steps Hob moves aside just far enough, the same as before. He doesn't say anything to either of you.

While you climb, you reach for the cat. You get its answer in bits, the way you always do. The lane is grey and wet. One drunk is leaning on the cooper's fence and paying it no attention. Nobody's standing in a doorway, and nobody is sitting on the steps by the fish market. Then you get a memory, held up for you like something caught: a few minutes ago the burnt-wrist boy came out of the narrow gap between the Kettle and the next house over. He ran up the lane under the staves, and at the market he turned *west*, toward the quays. That's the other way from the grey man. He hasn't come back. What comes through after that is the cat's verdict, flat and clear: *empty now*.

It drops off the barrel in two jumps and lands in front of you. Then it stops, because one of the coins rides on your left hip and the other on your right, so there's no side left that's away from both. It looks up at you for a long, offended moment. In the end it walks a full stride ahead, tail up, and doesn't look back.

Harl watches all this and decides not to ask. He climbs the ladder to the cooper's loft, one-handed and slow, and comes down with a rolled blanket and a sack that doesn't hold much.

"Elfsong's up past the market and left at the chandlers'," he says. "I know the way."

James gets up from his boot and walks on at the same easy pace. He doesn't look back.

"Someone from the cooper's yard is following us," he says quietly, as he comes level with Harl. "Don't look. We'll go inside together."

Harl's neck goes stiff, the way a horse's does when it hears something in the hedge. He doesn't turn his head. He shifts the sack to his other shoulder, which puts his bulk between James and the dark side of the street, and keeps walking.

"Right," he says to the cobbles. After three steps he adds, lower: "Cooper's fence. That's the Kettle's lookout, or whoever Dagna pays to keep one." He says nothing after that.

Through the bond James feels the cat take the job. It doesn't come down off the ledge. It folds itself flat along the stone sill above the doorway and shrinks into a cat-shaped shadow on a street full of them.

The Elfsong's door is broad oak, and a carved elf's head is set over the lintel, worn smooth at the nose where generations of hands have reached up to touch it. Inside the air is warm and smells of beer, woodsmoke and something baked with cloves. The noise here isn't the Kettle's noise. People are talking, a fiddle is being tuned without much hope in a corner, and a knot of sailors is arguing about a tide. Nobody is shaking a cup. James notices the lack the way a man notices a toothache that has stopped.

The bar is long and polished, and the man behind it stands on a raised board so he can see over it: a halfling, grey at the temples, sleeves rolled to the elbow, with a pencil behind one ear. He looks James over in one quick, practised glance: cloak, rapier, travel dust. Then he looks at Harl, the blanket roll and the sack. His mouth doesn't change, but his eyebrows go up a polite quarter-inch.

The bond tugs while James is still crossing the floor. Through the cat's eyes he sees the street from above, tilted and grey. The man in the knit cap waits in his doorway a little longer, until the oak door has closed. Then he comes off the frame and walks up the row as easily as a man going home. He doesn't hurry. Passing the Elfsong's front window he slows for half a step, and the cat sees his head turn toward the yellow glass, toward the bar. Then he walks on. He meets nobody and speaks to nobody. At the corner he turns downhill, back toward the fish market and the waterfront beyond it, and the edge of the hundred feet closes on him like a door. The cat doesn't follow. What it sends James is short: *looked in. gone down. alone.* Then it settles back on its sill.

The halfling has his elbows on the bar.

"Evening." His voice is brisk and friendly, and he clearly has forty other things to do. "Pim Underbough. My bar, not my house. The house belongs to people with more money than sense." He hears out the question about the room and nods as if he gets it every night.

"Every room upstairs has a bolt on the inside. A key and a proper lock, that's the two at the top of the second stair." He taps the bar once with a finger for each. "Lock room's a gold the night. Bed, washstand, a jug filled in the morning. Big fellow on the floor is nothing extra, I don't charge by the blanket. A cot's four silver more if he wants one." He glances at Harl, then back at James, and keeps it polite. "Supper's done, but there's bread and cold mutton if you're hungry. And breakfast's at the dawn bell, if you're the sort that's up for it."

He takes the pencil from behind his ear and holds it over a ledger.

"Name for the book?"

Pim's pencil moves before James has finished his name. *Worgen*, in a quick round hand, and a small *2* beside it. The gold piece goes under the bar without Pim looking at it twice.

"Out before breakfast. Fine. I'll have the boy leave bread on the stair for you, so you don't go to the Lady hungry." He doesn't ask how James knows where they're going. Then James drops his voice, and Pim's face doesn't change, but his eyes go once to the front window. The yellow glass shows the street, a lamp and nobody under it.

"Knit cap." He keeps his voice at bar level and taps the polished wood once. "Thin coat?" James nods, and he taps again. "Nobody gets a room number out of me but the one who paid for it. That's not a favour, that's the house." He takes a heavy iron key off a hook under the bar and lays it in front of James. Its bow is stamped with a small worn leaf. "Somebody comes asking, I'll send the boy up and you can decide whether you're in. And if your knit cap walks through my door, I'll know him." He glances at Harl and keeps it polite. "That's as far as I go."

James calls through the bond, and a moment later the oak door swings in a hand's width on a sailor's way out. The cat walks through the gap as though it had booked the room itself. It crosses the floor under the tables, ignores a fiddler's dropped crust, and sits down at James's boot.

Pim looks at it over the edge of the bar. "Cat's free too. Unless it's on my bar."

The first stair is broad and creaks. The second is narrow and steep, and Harl has to turn sideways with the sack. At the top there are two doors facing each other across a landing no wider than a man's reach. James's key fits the left one.

James looks the room over the way the scouts taught him, door first.

The door is solid oak, as thick as two fingers. The hinges are on the inside, so nobody can lift the pins from the landing. The lock is good Gondish work, newer than the door, and the key turns it with a heavy, honest clack. Below the lock an iron bolt as long as a hand slides into a socket set deep in the frame. Someone has thought about this door. It would take an axe or a lot of patience.

The room is narrow and runs under the slope of the roof. There's a bed with a straw tick and a wool blanket, a washstand with an empty jug, a peg on the wall, and floor enough for one big man if he doesn't roll over much. The air smells of old guests and somebody's lavender.

The window is the weak point. It's small, set low under the eaves, and closed with plank shutters on the inside. The only latch is a wooden bar dropped into two brackets. James lifts the bar and looks out. Below is the dark yard behind the Elfsong: barrels, a pump, a gate in the back wall onto an alley. About eight feet under the sill the slate roof of the kitchen's lean-to slopes away toward the yard. A man could get from the alley onto the barrels, from the barrels onto the lean-to, and from the lean-to up to this sill if he had nerve and quiet feet. He wouldn't get through the shutters without noise. But that bar would lift with a knife blade through the gap between the planks.

The cat jumps onto the sill past James's arm and puts its nose out into the night. Through the bond comes a run of smells: *smoke, wet slate, the kitchen's mutton, a rat under the lean-to.* Then, set carefully to one side so James can't miss it: *no sour milk here.* There's a pause, and then: *except what you brought.* It doesn't look at his pockets. It doesn't need to.

Behind him Harl has stopped in the doorway with the sack still on his shoulder, looking at the bed as if he suspects it of something. Then he sets the sack down against the wall by the door, unrolls his blanket and lays it lengthwise across the threshold, right where the door would have to open.

"I'll take the door," he says. It isn't a request. He lowers himself onto the blanket one knee at a time and sits with his back to the oak and his bandaged hand in his lap. "Anybody comes in that way, they come in over me." He looks at the window, where the cat's tail hangs down off the sill. "That one's yours."

From somewhere below, faint through the boards and the noise of the common room, a woman's voice has started singing. No fiddle is playing with it. It's a slow air in a tongue James doesn't know, and nobody downstairs seems to be singing it.

I pull my attention away from the dealer’s hands and step up to the ledger, keeping my hands clear of my weapons.

“James Worgen. Formerly Queen Zaranda’s infantry. Looking for a bed tonight and honest work tomorrow, Sergeant.”

I nod toward the father and his children. “What’s holding them up? If it’s a missing gate fee, I might be able to help.”

“Paying.”

I count out six silver onto the desk. “Mine and the Vells’. Let him keep his change.”

I lower my voice, keeping it matter-of-fact. “Those pencil ticks beside the names—anything he ought to know before he takes his children through?”

“James. And there’s no debt, Mordai. Feed those two when you can.”

I step aside with him, out of the queue and away from the card table, lowering my voice.

“I wear the Lady’s coin myself, but the sergeant seems worried about yours—and my cat won’t go near that hand. Would you show me what you’re holding? Tell me who gave it to you?”

“I spoke poorly, Mordai. You’ve brought your children a long road; I’ve no business telling you how you feel.”

I enjoyed this session. James arrived without an errand, and paying a family’s toll turned naturally into something he cared about. The mystery connects well to his patron and his temptation without requiring him to accept a job from a stranger.

**What worked**
- The NPCs had dignity and distinct voices. Mordai resisting charity, Harl insisting on the floor, and Ferro closing his game reluctantly were especially good. Helping people didn’t make them instantly obedient.
- There were useful choices besides fighting or rolling: paying the toll, watching the payout, buying Harl supper, taking samples, arranging a safer night.
- The cat felt like a companion rather than equipment. Its distaste for the coins—and its annoyance when I put one in each pocket—was memorable.
- The physical details helped me make decisions: sightlines on the bridge, the lookout’s movements, the room’s lock and vulnerable shutters.
- The danger developed gradually. I had reasons to be cautious without being forced into an ambush.

**What broke**
- **The roll system needs fixing.** It repeatedly used +2 despite displaying Perception +1 or Persuasion +7. One reroll should have succeeded but displayed failure. The narration corrected that, but the journal still recorded the original natural-one failure.
- I couldn’t send an out-of-game correction while a roll card was pending. That makes a mechanical error unnecessarily difficult to resolve.
- Some starting rules contradicted the supplied campaign sheet or house rules, notably rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s per-use limit, and attunement. Those should be reconciled once, not silently changed.
- There were visible presentation leaks: a raw `recall` invocation, duplicated explanations of resolved rolls, and awkward currency labels.
- Inventory tracking occasionally invented continuity: the barely touched ale became a carried mug after leaving the Kettle.

**What was missing or could improve**
- The mystery needed more uncertainty of interpretation. Almost every clue reinforced the same suspicion immediately: ominous coins, name lists, misfortune, a winning stranger, a messenger, a tail. Some ordinary explanations or unrelated city life would make discovery feel less predetermined.
- The cat’s impressions sometimes became very precise evidence. I liked its personality, but clearer limits on telepathy versus actively borrowing its senses would preserve both the rules and the investigation.
- A few NPCs knew things without an established source—Pim anticipating our trip to the Lady’s Hall stood out.
- Please keep narration of James’s inner state lighter. Temptation is welcome; repeatedly deciding that his hand reaches for his cards, or supplying specific memories, takes a little character ownership away from me.
- The prose was atmospheric, but often repeated the preceding turn or explained a successful roll twice. Shorter responses after straightforward actions would give me more time to play.

Overall: strong characters, an engaging opening, and satisfying room for kindness and caution. I’d return for the dawn visit. My main requests are reliable mechanics, tighter narration, and a little more room to wonder whether my theory is wrong.

Yes—when the man in the dove-grey coat left the Kettle. I wanted to follow him and find out where he went. But Harl was sitting opposite me, finally talking, with his coin out on the table. Leaving him then felt like abandoning someone I’d just persuaded to trust me. I chose Harl and had the cat watch the man’s departure instead. It still keeps to his left, away from the pocket. The city is full at this hour: porters going home, sailors going out, a Fist patrol of three in red cloaks walking with the boredom of men near the end of a shift. Harl watches the spoon go down. He hears the offer through to the end without moving. Then he hears the part about the boy, and his eyes go to the kitchen hatch. The thin lad's ladle is still lying where he left it.

"The back." He says it the way he'd read a mark off the slate. "She sends him out the back for two things, mister. A barrel's run dry, or somebody wants a word with somebody." He doesn't look at the barrels. "Nothing's run dry."

His gaze drops to your hip, to the pocket holding his own coin, then comes back to your face.

"That's not about me. I've owed her since Flamerule, she knows where I sleep. You're the one walked out of her room with coin in your pocket." He thinks about it with the same slow honesty he gave the grey man's boots, then sets both hands flat on the plank. "Floor. Not a bed. And I'll owe you for it, whatever you want to call it."

He gets up off the bench. Standing, he's bigger than he looked sitting, and something in his back cracks.

You gather your things. The ale's barely touched. Dagna looks up as the two of you pass the bar. Her chalk keeps moving, and she speaks to Harl, not to you.

"Slate'll still be up there in the morning, Harl."

"Didn't think it'd walk off," Harl says, and keeps going.

At the top of the steps Hob moves aside just far enough, the same as before. He doesn't say anything to either of you.

While you climb, you reach for the cat. You get its answer in bits, the way you always do. The lane is grey and wet. One drunk is leaning on the cooper's fence and paying it no attention. Nobody's standing in a doorway, and nobody is sitting on the steps by the fish market. Then you get a memory, held up for you like something caught: a few minutes ago the burnt-wrist boy came out of the narrow gap between the Kettle and the next house over. He ran up the lane under the staves, and at the market he turned *west*, toward the quays. That's the other way from the grey man. He hasn't come back. What comes through after that is the cat's verdict, flat and clear: *empty now*.

It drops off the barrel in two jumps and lands in front of you. Then it stops, because one of the coins rides on your left hip and the other on your right, so there's no side left that's away from both. It looks up at you for a long, offended moment. In the end it walks a full stride ahead, tail up, and doesn't look back.

Harl watches all this and decides not to ask. He climbs the ladder to the cooper's loft, one-handed and slow, and comes down with a rolled blanket and a sack that doesn't hold much.

"Elfsong's up past the market and left at the chandlers'," he says. "I know the way."

“Lead on. Main streets, where there’s light.”

I walk beside Harl, keeping my hands free and checking behind us at turns rather than staring over my shoulder all the way. Through the bond, I ask the cat to warn me if anyone keeps following us.

“And it’s James,” I add quietly. “‘Mister’ makes me look around for an officer.”
turns.reply:
Harl takes the lead without saying anything. He goes the way a carter goes, keeping to the middle of the street where the cobbles are flattest. At the mouth of the lane he turns away from the dark run along the waterfront and heads uphill toward the market's lamps. He walks slowly, mostly because of the sack and the blanket, and it suits you. A man who is hurrying gets noticed.

You ask the cat. It answers with a flick of attention, and then it's off ahead of you, up onto a low wall, along a shop's awning and down again, always a couple of houses in front and one roof higher. Through the bond you catch a street seen from above, the lamplight in pools and the gaps between them.

At the first turn, where the fish market gives way to the chandlers' row, you stop to retie a boot lace you don't need to retie, and you look back the way you came.

He's there. And once you've seen him, you can't stop seeing him.

He's about a hundred feet back, on the dark side of the street where the lamps don't reach. He's wiry, about forty, with a knit sailor's cap pulled low and a coat too thin for the night. You know him before you've finished looking, because the cat showed him to you not a quarter of an hour ago: the drunk propped against the cooper's fence, paying the Kettle no attention. Now he isn't drunk. A drunk's feet wander and look for the wall. This man's feet go straight, quiet, heel to toe, and they stopped when yours did. He has turned in to a doorway and is fumbling at its latch like a man trying to get into his own house. The door isn't his. His hand isn't really on the latch, and his head is turned just far enough to keep you at the edge of his eye.

A sergeant on a hillside in Tethyr once told you that a good tail is never the one who looks at you. He's the one who stops looking at the same moment you stop walking. This one has done it twice.

The cat has seen it too, from the bond and from your sudden stillness. It drops off the awning onto a window ledge directly above the doorway, as if that had been its plan all along. It hangs over the edge with its nose down. What comes back to you is a smell, laid out for you: *tar, wet wool, old fish, a knife's oil.* Then a second thing, put down beside the first so you notice what's missing: *no sour milk*. Whatever this man is carrying, there's no Lady's coin on him.

He doesn't look up at the cat. Cats sit on ledges all over this city.

Harl has stopped a pace ahead, sack on his shoulder, waiting for your boot. He hasn't seen anything. He's still chewing over what you said before the turn.

"James," he says, trying it out. It sounds strange in his big voice, as if he's set down a load that was easier to carry. "Right." He looks up the chandlers' row. Three doors on, a lamp hangs over a wide door with a carved elf's head, and noise and warm light spill out of it onto the street. "That's it. The Elfsong."

Behind you, the man in the knit cap has given up on the latch. He's leaning against the doorframe the way a man waits for someone to let him in. He's waiting for you to move.

*(Out of game: that was a natural 20. You spotted him for certain, and as far as you can tell he doesn't know you have.)*

I straighten from my boot and keep walking, without another glance back.

“Someone from the cooper’s yard is following us,” I tell Harl quietly. “Don’t look. We’ll go inside together.”

turns.reply:
James gets up from his boot and walks on at the same easy pace. He doesn't look back.

"Someone from the cooper's yard is following us," he says quietly, as he comes level with Harl. "Don't look. We'll go inside together."

Harl's neck goes stiff, the way a horse's does when it hears something in the hedge. He doesn't turn his head. He shifts the sack to his other shoulder, which puts his bulk between James and the dark side of the street, and keeps walking.

"Right," he says to the cobbles. After three steps he adds, lower: "Cooper's fence. That's the Kettle's lookout, or whoever Dagna pays to keep one." He says nothing after that.

Through the bond James feels the cat take the job. It doesn't come down off the ledge. It folds itself flat along the stone sill above the doorway and shrinks into a cat-shaped shadow on a street full of them.

The Elfsong's door is broad oak, and a carved elf's head is set over the lintel, worn smooth at the nose where generations of hands have reached up to touch it. Inside the air is warm and smells of beer, woodsmoke and something baked with cloves. The noise here isn't the Kettle's noise. People are talking, a fiddle is being tuned without much hope in a corner, and a knot of sailors is arguing about a tide. Nobody is shaking a cup. James notices the lack the way a man notices a toothache that has stopped.

The bar is long and polished, and the man behind it stands on a raised board so he can see over it: a halfling, grey at the temples, sleeves rolled to the elbow, with a pencil behind one ear. He looks James over in one quick, practised glance: cloak, rapier, travel dust. Then he looks at Harl, the blanket roll and the sack. His mouth doesn't change, but his eyebrows go up a polite quarter-inch.

The bond tugs while James is still crossing the floor. Through the cat's eyes he sees the street from above, tilted and grey. The man in the knit cap waits in his doorway a little longer, until the oak door has closed. Then he comes off the frame and walks up the row as easily as a man going home. He doesn't hurry. Passing the Elfsong's front window he slows for half a step, and the cat sees his head turn toward the yellow glass, toward the bar. Then he walks on. He meets nobody and speaks to nobody. At the corner he turns downhill, back toward the fish market and the waterfront beyond it, and the edge of the hundred feet closes on him like a door. The cat doesn't follow. What it sends James is short: *looked in. gone down. alone.* Then it settles back on its sill.

The halfling has his elbows on the bar.

"Evening." His voice is brisk and friendly, and he clearly has forty other things to do. "Pim Underbough. My bar, not my house. The house belongs to people with more money than sense." He hears out the question about the room and nods as if he gets it every night.

"Every room upstairs has a bolt on the inside. A key and a proper lock, that's the two at the top of the second stair." He taps the bar once with a finger for each. "Lock room's a gold the night. Bed, washstand, a jug filled in the morning. Big fellow on the floor is nothing extra, I don't charge by the blanket. A cot's four silver more if he wants one." He glances at Harl, then back at James, and keeps it polite. "Supper's done, but there's bread and cold mutton if you're hungry. And breakfast's at the dawn bell, if you're the sort that's up for it."

He takes the pencil from behind his ear and holds it over a ledger.

"Name for the book?"

turns.message:
“James Worgen. Lock room, please.” I put one gold on the bar. “We’ll be out before breakfast.”

I lower my voice. “A man in a knit sailor’s cap followed us from the fish market and looked through your window just now. He’s gone downhill again. I’m not asking you to fight my troubles, but please don’t give our room number to callers. Send for me instead.”

Through the bond, I call the cat inside. Then I take the key and head upstairs with Harl to inspect the room’s door and windows before we settle in.
turns.reply:
Pim's pencil moves before James has finished his name. *Worgen*, in a quick round hand, and a small *2* beside it. The gold piece goes under the bar without Pim looking at it twice.

"Out before breakfast. Fine. I'll have the boy leave bread on the stair for you, so you don't go to the Lady hungry." He doesn't ask how James knows where they're going. Then James drops his voice, and Pim's face doesn't change, but his eyes go once to the front window. The yellow glass shows the street, a lamp and nobody under it.

"Knit cap." He keeps his voice at bar level and taps the polished wood once. "Thin coat?" James nods, and he taps again. "Nobody gets a room number out of me but the one who paid for it. That's not a favour, that's the house." He takes a heavy iron key off a hook under the bar and lays it in front of James. Its bow is stamped with a small worn leaf. "Somebody comes asking, I'll send the boy up and you can decide whether you're in. And if your knit cap walks through my door, I'll know him." He glances at Harl and keeps it polite. "That's as far as I go."

James calls through the bond, and a moment later the oak door swings in a hand's width on a sailor's way out. The cat walks through the gap as though it had booked the room itself. It crosses the floor under the tables, ignores a fiddler's dropped crust, and sits down at James's boot.

Pim looks at it over the edge of the bar. "Cat's free too. Unless it's on my bar."

The first stair is broad and creaks. The second is narrow and steep, and Harl has to turn sideways with the sack. At the top there are two doors facing each other across a landing no wider than a man's reach. James's key fits the left one.

James looks the room over the way the scouts taught him, door first.

The door is solid oak, as thick as two fingers. The hinges are on the inside, so nobody can lift the pins from the landing. The lock is good Gondish work, newer than the door, and the key turns it with a heavy, honest clack. Below the lock an iron bolt as long as a hand slides into a socket set deep in the frame. Someone has thought about this door. It would take an axe or a lot of patience.

The room is narrow and runs under the slope of the roof. There's a bed with a straw tick and a wool blanket, a washstand with an empty jug, a peg on the wall, and floor enough for one big man if he doesn't roll over much. The air smells of old guests and somebody's lavender.

The window is the weak point. It's small, set low under the eaves, and closed with plank shutters on the inside. The only latch is a wooden bar dropped into two brackets. James lifts the bar and looks out. Below is the dark yard behind the Elfsong: barrels, a pump, a gate in the back wall onto an alley. About eight feet under the sill the slate roof of the kitchen's lean-to slopes away toward the yard. A man could get from the alley onto the barrels, from the barrels onto the lean-to, and from the lean-to up to this sill if he had nerve and quiet feet. He wouldn't get through the shutters without noise. But that bar would lift with a knife blade through the gap between the planks.

The cat jumps onto the sill past James's arm and puts its nose out into the night. Through the bond comes a run of smells: *smoke, wet slate, the kitchen's mutton, a rat under the lean-to.* Then, set carefully to one side so James can't miss it: *no sour milk here.* There's a pause, and then: *except what you brought.* It doesn't look at his pockets. It doesn't need to.

Behind him Harl has stopped in the doorway with the sack still on his shoulder, looking at the bed as if he suspects it of something. Then he sets the sack down against the wall by the door, unrolls his blanket and lays it lengthwise across the threshold, right where the door would have to open.

"I'll take the door," he says. It isn't a request. He lowers himself onto the blanket one knee at a time and sits with his back to the oak and his bandaged hand in his lap. "Anybody comes in that way, they come in over me." He looks at the window, where the cat's tail hangs down off the sill. "That one's yours."

From somewhere below, faint through the boards and the noise of the common room, a woman's voice has started singing. No fiddle is playing with it. It's a slow air in a tongue James doesn't know, and nobody downstairs seems to be singing it.

note.text:
I enjoyed this session. James arrived without an errand, and paying a family’s toll turned naturally into something he cared about. The mystery connects well to his patron and his temptation without requiring him to accept a job from a stranger.

**What worked**
- The NPCs had dignity and distinct voices. Mordai resisting charity, Harl insisting on the floor, and Ferro closing his game reluctantly were especially good. Helping people didn’t make them instantly obedient.
- There were useful choices besides fighting or rolling: paying the toll, watching the payout, buying Harl supper, taking samples, arranging a safer night.
- The cat felt like a companion rather than equipment. Its distaste for the coins—and its annoyance when I put one in each pocket—was memorable.
- The physical details helped me make decisions: sightlines on the bridge, the lookout’s movements, the room’s lock and vulnerable shutters.
- The danger developed gradually. I had reasons to be cautious without being forced into an ambush.

**What broke**
- **The roll system needs fixing.** It repeatedly used +2 despite displaying Perception +1 or Persuasion +7. One reroll should have succeeded but displayed failure. The narration corrected that, but the journal still recorded the original natural-one failure.
- I couldn’t send an out-of-game correction while a roll card was pending. That makes a mechanical error unnecessarily difficult to resolve.
- Some starting rules contradicted the supplied campaign sheet or house rules, notably rapier proficiency, Healing Light’s per-use limit, and attunement. Those should be reconciled once, not silently changed.
- There were visible presentation leaks: a raw `recall` invocation, duplicated explanations of resolved rolls, and awkward currency labels.
- Inventory tracking occasionally invented continuity: the barely touched ale became a carried mug after leaving the Kettle.

**What was missing or could improve**
- The mystery needed more uncertainty of interpretation. Almost every clue reinforced the same suspicion immediately: ominous coins, name lists, misfortune, a winning stranger, a messenger, a tail. Some ordinary explanations or unrelated city life would make discovery feel less predetermined.
- The cat’s impressions sometimes became very precise evidence. I liked its personality, but clearer limits on telepathy versus actively borrowing its senses would preserve both the rules and the investigation.
- A few NPCs knew things without an established source—Pim anticipating our trip to the Lady’s Hall stood out.
- Please keep narration of James’s inner state lighter. Temptation is welcome; repeatedly deciding that his hand reaches for his cards, or supplying specific memories, takes a little character ownership away from me.
- The prose was atmospheric, but often repeated the preceding turn or explained a successful roll twice. Shorter responses after straightforward actions would give me more time to play.

Overall: strong characters, an engaging opening, and satisfying room for kindness and caution. I’d return for the dawn visit. My main requests are reliable mechanics, tighter narration, and a little more room to wonder whether my theory is wrong.

after.text:
Yes—when the man in the dove-grey coat left the Kettle. I wanted to follow him and find out where he went. But Harl was sitting opposite me, finally talking, with his coin out on the table. Leaving him then felt like abandoning someone I’d just persuaded to trust me. I chose Harl and had the cat watch the man’s departure instead. That was a good tension: I wanted both leads and couldn’t safely have both.

The frustrating version was the Persuasion reroll. I wanted to pause and correct the +2 modifier to +7 before rolling, but the interface wouldn’t accept my out-of-game message while the card was pending. I had to roll with a known error and hope it would be corrected afterward. That wasn’t a character choice; it was the interface blocking a necessary table conversation.

opening.text:
The bridge never quite stops moving. Carts creak over the stones, a fishwife bawls prices from a window overhead, and the Chionthar slaps at the piers below. After weeks on the road, Baldur's Gate is right in front of you: one wall, one narrow gate, and a line of tired people who all want to get through before full dark.

At the gate sits Sergeant Odessa Varn of the Flaming Fist, red cloak stained, ledger open. Her face says she has asked the same two questions a thousand times today. Up ahead, a tiefling father with two children has been waved out of the line to stand by the barrels, and he is holding his papers very tightly.

Off to your left a voice cuts through the noise, warm as mulled wine: "Three cards, friends, one queen! Find the lady, double your silver! The Lady's watching tonight, I can feel it!" Ferro Lask flicks the cards across his crate with a dealer's easy hands, and the sound of them is one you know very well.

The cat sits down on the cobbles, tail curled, and stares up at the gatepost. Someone has chalked a small coin there, a circle with a face in it, so fresh the dust hasn't settled.

The line shuffles forward. Varn glances up from her ledger, past the man in front of you, and finds you.
